name: Alloy Orange
lede: Alloy Orange is a deep, brownish orange from Crayola's crayon list, close enough to the older name [[burnt-orange|burnt orange]] that the two are easy to mistake on screen.

sections.title: A Crayola name with no paper trail
sections.body: Alloy Orange sits in Crayola's crayon list, and our only record of it traces to Wikipedia's inventory of Crayola names rather than to any dictionary or color standard in our library [1]. Crayola does not publish an explanation for the name, so when the crayon was introduced and who chose the name are both undocumented here [1]. The ISCC-NBS system classifies this hex value as a deep orange, about 2.1 units from that block's reference chip, and its Munsell notation works out to 3.6YR 5.1/11.7 [2].

sections.title: Nearly burnt orange
sections.body: Our library's own color match places Alloy Orange within about 4.3 units of [[burnt-orange|burnt orange]], which reads a little more vivid beside it [2]. Closer still, at 3.8 units, are [[rust-orange|Orange-Rufous]] and [[rust-orange|rust orange]], near twins on a screen, with the lighter [[xanthine-orange|Xanthine Orange]] just beyond at 3.9 [2]. The two names have unrelated histories: burnt orange is dated as early as 1915 and entered the 1930 Maerz and Paul dictionary, while Alloy Orange has no comparable record, only Crayola's own choice [2][3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color near Alloy Orange appears in 141, about 0.59 per cent, and in 103 by the stricter within-painting measure, which is more common than 59 per cent of the named colors we track [4]. It functions almost entirely as an accent, 88 per cent of those 103 paintings, a small warm note rather than a field of color [4].

It peaks in paintings from the 1500s, at 1.4 times the expected rate, and is most over-represented in paintings from India, at 3.8 times expected [4]. These are photographs of varnished paintings read as screen colors, most painted centuries before Crayola existed, so the match is a hue coincidence, not a use of this crayon [4].
